intro: The six hand-checked guides were researched by an AI agent (Claude) reading provider docs, then cross-checked claim by claim. Where docs and the wider web disagreed, we kept the official source and recorded the conflict here. A person then tried parts of the setup in real consoles. Generated guides go through an automated version of the same discipline: every fact must carry a quote, and quotes not found on the source page are marked uncertain.

attempts.what: Registered an OAuth app (personal account) with Composio's callback URL, 2026-10-27.
observed: The form page is titled “Register a new OAuth app”.

The callback field is now a “Redirect URIs” section with an “Add redirect URI” button and the text “You may add up to 10 redirect URIs”. GitHub's docs still call it “Authorization callback URL”, so the guide now uses the on-screen wording.
Each redirect URI has its own “Allow wildcard matching” checkbox, unticked by default.
“Expire user access tokens” was ticked by default, with the note that it provides a refresh_token.
After clicking Register: “Application created successfully”, a Client ID shown immediately, “0 users”, and a client secret generated on demand. No review or pending state.
After creation, the expiry checkbox no longer appears on the General page; the left menu has General, Optional features and Advanced.

attempts.what: Create an app from scratch, add the redirect URL, open Manage Distribution.
New project → Google Auth Platform → add gmail.readonly → inspect Audience and the publish flow (without publishing).

checks.claim: GitHub's form field is called “Authorization callback URL”.
checks.finding: Found only by actually trying it: GitHub's docs still say “Authorization callback URL”, but the live form shows a “Redirect URIs” section with per-URI wildcard checkboxes. The guide uses the on-screen wording so developers don't get stuck looking for a field that isn't there.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Creating an OAuth app

checks.claim: GitHub OAuth app tokens never expire, and an OAuth app has a single callback URL.
checks.finding: Out of date. Since GitHub's August 14, 2026 change, new OAuth apps issue 8-hour tokens with 6-month refresh tokens by default and accept up to 10 callback URLs. Popular libraries' docs still describe the old behaviour.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: Creating an OAuth app

checks.claim: Any user can connect their org's repos once they authorize your OAuth app.
checks.finding: New organizations have OAuth app access restrictions on by default. Members can only request approval, and an org owner must approve. We added this as the GitHub launch gate.

sources.title: GitHub Docs: OAuth app access restrictions

checks.claim: Marketplace submission requires 5 active workspace installs.
checks.finding: A recent third-party article (Aug 2026) quotes 5. Slack's own review guide says 10 active workspaces (used in the past 28 days) and blocks submission below that. We use 10.

checks.claim: The 1-request-per-minute history limit only affects new installs of unlisted apps.
checks.finding: True when announced (May 2025), but Slack's changelog says existing installs of unlisted distributed apps moved to the new limits on March 3, 2026.
Preliminary review up to 10 business days; functional review up to 10 weeks for new apps (6 for updates). Resubmitting during the preliminary phase resets your queue position.

checks.claim: Brand verification takes 2–3 business days; sensitive scopes 3–5 business days.
checks.finding: Both figures appear on Google's own production-readiness pages.

checks.claim: Restricted-scope (Gmail read) verification takes N weeks.
checks.finding: Google publishes no fixed timeline; we only found “several weeks or longer” attributed to Google by third parties. The guide says so and marks our 42-day scoring estimate as ours.

checks.claim: CASA Tier 2 can be done with a free self-scan.
checks.finding: 2024 forum posts show Google offering a self-scan option; 2025–26 sources say a lab-verified assessment is required. The guide recommends budgeting for an authorized lab and lists this as uncertain.

checks.claim: Unlisted HubSpot apps are capped at 25 installs.
checks.finding: Confirmed for marketplace-distribution OAuth apps on the 2025.2+ platform (developer test accounts excluded), enforced since September 22, 2025.
Only found in a partner agency's write-up, which itself warns HubSpot has changed the threshold before. Marked third-party in the guide.

checks.claim: Posting on a member's behalf (w_member_social) needs partner verification.
checks.finding: A third-party guide claims so, but LinkedIn's own docs list Share on LinkedIn as a self-serve product you add in the portal. Company-page posting is the gated part.

checks.claim: Access tokens last 60 days; refresh tokens 365 days.
checks.finding: Stated in LinkedIn's docs, but the sample responses' expires_in values don't match those durations in seconds. The guide tells developers to check a live response, and notes refresh tokens are partner-only.

checks.claim: Public integrations must pass Notion's review before other workspaces can install them.
checks.finding: Review applies only to Marketplace listings (5–10 business days). A public connection works via OAuth without being listed.

checks.claim: There is one Composio callback URL.
checks.finding: Composio's docs show three: /api/v3/toolkits/auth/callback (white-labeling guide), /api/v3.1/… (some preview docs) and the legacy /api/v1/auth-apps/add. Guides use v3, and tell developers to copy the exact URI from their Composio auth config.

learned: The real question isn't “how do I create the app?” (minutes everywhere) but “what gates production?”, and the answer is different per provider: security audits (Google), install caps (HubSpot), rate limits (Slack), partner vetting (LinkedIn), customer-side admin approval (GitHub). So each guide leads with the gate, not the steps.
Scope choice often matters more than the provider: Gmail send-only is days, Gmail read is weeks plus an annual paid audit. We added “Pick your path” blocks so developers see this before writing code.

Provider rules changed a lot in the last 18 months (GitHub tokens, Slack limits, HubSpot caps). Third-party guides and model memory lag behind, so the live agent always reads current pages and dates every source.

Composio's managed apps remove the approval wait during development, but connections are tied to the app they were made with. Moving users to your own app later forces everyone to reconnect. Every guide says when to switch.
Model-written “quotes” sometimes aren't on the page. We now check every quote against the fetched text and downgrade unmatched claims to uncertain instead of trusting them.
pipeline: Check Composio's public toolkit page for managed-OAuth availability.
Run four targeted searches (create app, OAuth docs, app review, verification and limits) and rank results: the provider's own domains first, at most two third-party pages.
Fetch pages and keep only paragraphs about OAuth, review, limits and timelines (keyword scoring, no LLM) to fit the free-tier token budget.
Probe live endpoints without an account: the OpenID discovery document, and the real authorize endpoint called with a fake client_id to observe the error a developer will see.
Extract facts per page with a small model. Each fact must include a verbatim quote, which code then checks against the page text.
Write the guide with a larger model from the numbered facts only, citing fact IDs. Uncited claims are marked uncertain.
Compute difficulty with the fixed rubric from extracted flags, never from the model's opinion.
limitations: Generated guides are a first draft: they're only as good as the pages search surfaces, and providers with login-walled docs produce thin guides.
The free Groq tier rate-limits tokens per model, so a live run takes about 1–3 minutes and only two runs happen at once.
DuckDuckGo search may throttle cloud servers; set TAVILY_API_KEY for reliable search, or paste the provider's docs URL instead of a name.
On Render's free plan the disk isn't persistent, so generated guides disappear on redeploy (curated guides ship in the repo).
“Tested” claims cover only the console steps a person actually tried; no app was submitted for real provider review.
Difficulty scoring is deliberately simple and transparent. Two providers with the same score can still feel different.
